\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The setting}
Fix the field $\Laur$ of formal Laurent series: expressions $x=\sum_{n\in\ZZ}x_nq^n$ with $x_n\in\CC$ and $\{n:x_n\ne0\}$ bounded below. Equivalently, $\Laur$ is the Hahn series field with value group $\ZZ$ and coefficient field $\CC$; the general Hahn construction with an arbitrary ordered abelian value group will matter in Sections~\ref{sec:puiseux}--\ref{sec:interp}.

For $x\ne0$ write $\ord(x)\in\ZZ$ for the least exponent with $x_{\ord(x)}\ne0$, and $\lc(x)=x_{\ord(x)}$ for the leading coefficient. It is convenient also to use $\ordt$, taking values in $\ZZ\cup\{\infty\}$ with $\ordt(0)=\infty$, so that $\ordt$ is a genuine valuation on all of $\Laur$:
\[
\ordt(xy)=\ordt(x)+\ordt(y),\qquad \ordt(x+y)\ge\min\{\ordt(x),\ordt(y)\}.
\]

\subsection{Normalized series}

\begin{definition}[Normalized series]\label{def:norm}
A Laurent series $f\in\Laur$ is \emph{normalized} if $f_{-1}=1$ and $f_n=0$ for all $n<-1$; equivalently $f=q^{-1}+\sum_{n\ge0}c_nq^n$ for a sequence $(c_n)_{n\ge0}$ of complex numbers, its \emph{tail}. We write $\mathcal T(c)$ for the normalized series with tail $c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Corrected part]\label{def:corr}
For $f$ normalized, its \emph{corrected part} is the power series $\widehat f=qf\in\Pow$, so that $\widehat f=1+c_0q+c_1q^2+\cdots$ and $\widehat f_k=f_{k-1}$. In particular $\widehat f$ has constant term $1$.
\end{definition}

The motivating instance is monstrous moonshine: each conjugacy class $g$ of the Monster group carries a McKay--Thompson series $T_g(q)=q^{-1}+\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{tr}(g\mid V_n)q^{n}$, normalized in exactly the above sense, and there are $194$ such classes. We write $M=194$ for that class count. \emph{No property of the actual moonshine coefficients is used anywhere below}: all results are universally quantified over the tails, so the moonshine product is a special case, and the content is that the phenomena are consequences of shape and of the value group, not of arithmetic depth.

\subsection{The basic theorem and the question it decides}

\begin{theorem}[Pole-Order Theorem]\label{thm:pole}
Let $s$ be a finite index set and let $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ be normalized. Then
\[
\ordt\Big(\prod_{i\in s}f_i\Big)=-|s|.
\]
In particular the product is nonzero, has a pole of order exactly $|s|$, and has leading coefficient $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each factor has $\ordt=-1$ and the valuation is additive over finite products. Nonvanishing follows since the order is finite, and the leading coefficient is the product of the leading coefficients, all equal to $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Factorization]\label{cor:fact}
For normalized $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ with $m=|s|$,
\[
\prod_{i\in s}f_i=q^{-m}\cdot U,\qquad U=\prod_{i\in s}\widehat{f_i}\in\Pow,\quad U(0)=1.
\]
Multiplying by $q^m$ restores order $0$.
\end{corollary}

For the Monster-sized product this reads $\ord\big(\prod_gT_g\big)=-194$. Everything below flows from a single question: for which $n\ge1$ does there exist $y$ with $y^n=\prod_gT_g$? Additivity gives the necessary condition $n\mid194$ at once; Sections~\ref{sec:mult}--\ref{sec:root} show sufficiency, Sections~\ref{sec:rigid}--\ref{sec:comb} explore what else the invariant controls, and Sections~\ref{sec:repl}--\ref{sec:interp} change the ambient value group and watch the answer change.

\section{The multiplicative structure of $\Laur^{\times}$}\label{sec:mult}

\subsection{Splitting the valuation sequence}

\begin{theorem}[Splitting Theorem]\label{thm:split}
The map $\ZZ\times\Pow^{\times}\to\Laur^{\times}$, $(k,u)\mapsto q^ku$, is a group isomorphism, and under it $\ord$ is the projection onto the first factor.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
It is a homomorphism because $\ord(q^ku)=k$ and monomial exponents add. \emph{Injectivity:} if $q^ku=1$ then comparing orders gives $k=0$, hence $u=1$. \emph{Surjectivity:} for $x\ne0$ write $x=q^{\ord(x)}\pi(x)$ with the \emph{power-series part} $\pi(x)=q^{-\ord(x)}x$ of order $0$; its constant term is $\lc(x)\ne0$, so $\pi(x)\in\Pow^{\times}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exactness]\label{cor:exact}
$\ker(\ord)=\Pow^{\times}$ inside $\Laur^{\times}$: a Laurent series has order $0$ if and only if it is a unit power series.
\end{corollary}

Thus $1\to\Pow^{\times}\to\Laur^{\times}\xrightarrow{\ord}\ZZ\to0$ is split exact: any multiplicative question about $\Laur^{\times}$ decomposes into a question about $\ZZ$ and a question about $\Pow^{\times}$, and the second turns out to be vacuous.

\subsection{Roots of unit power series}

\begin{proposition}[Binomial roots]\label{prop:binom}
Let $u\in\Pow$ with $u(0)=1$ and let $n\ge1$. There exists $w\in\Pow$ with $w(0)=1$ and $w^n=u$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $B_r(X)=\sum_{k\ge0}\binom{r}{k}X^k$ be the binomial series, defined for $r\in\QQ$ because $\CC$ has characteristic zero. One has the formal identity $B_r(X)^k=B_{rk}(X)$, so $B_{1/n}(X)^n=1+X$. Now $a:=u-1$ has zero constant term, hence is substitutable, and $w:=B_{1/n}(a)$ satisfies $w^n=1+a=u$ with $w(0)=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:psroot}
If $P\in\Pow$ has $P(0)\ne0$ and $n\ge1$, then $P$ has an $n$-th root in $\Pow$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $P=P(0)u$ with $u(0)=1$, choose $\lambda$ with $\lambda^n=P(0)$ by algebraic closedness, and apply Proposition~\ref{prop:binom}; then $(\lambda w)^n=P$.
\end{proof}

Characteristic zero enters through the binomial coefficients, algebraic closedness through $\lambda$. Over $\CC$ both are available, and the power-series factor offers no obstruction at all.

\section{The root-extraction theorem}\label{sec:root}

\begin{theorem}[Root-Extraction Theorem]\label{thm:root}
Let $x\in\Laur$ be nonzero and let $n\ge1$. Then
\[
\exists\,y\in\Laur:\ y^n=x \iff n\mid\ord(x).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) If $y^n=x$ then $y\ne0$ and $\ord(x)=n\ord(y)$. ($\Leftarrow$) Write $\ord(x)=nk$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:split}, $x=q^{nk}\pi(x)$ with $\pi(x)$ a unit power series; by Corollary~\ref{cor:psroot} choose $w$ with $w^n=\pi(x)$. Then $y=q^kw$ satisfies $y^n=x$.
\end{proof}

The content is that the \emph{only} obstruction is arithmetic: no condition on the coefficients of $x$ intervenes.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:specnorm}
For normalized $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ with $m=|s|$ and $n\ge1$: $\exists\,y:y^n=\prod_{i\in s}f_i$ if and only if $n\mid m$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Monster root spectrum]\label{cor:monster}
For any tails $c_1,\dots,c_{194}$ and any $n\ge1$,
\[
\exists\,y:\ y^n=\prod_{i=1}^{194}\mathcal T(c_i) \iff n\mid194 \iff n\in\{1,2,97,194\}.
\]
In particular the product \emph{is} a square; it has \emph{no} cube root ($3\nmid194$) and \emph{no} fourth root ($194=2\cdot97$ is squarefree).
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Power classes: the invariant is complete and sharp}

Since $\Laur^{\times}$ is abelian, the subgroup $(\Laur^{\times})^n$ of $n$-th powers is normal, and $\ord$ descends modulo $n$ to $\overline{\ord}_n:\Laur^{\times}\to\ZZ/n\ZZ$.

\begin{theorem}[Classification of power classes]\label{thm:classes}
For every $n\ge1$,
\[
\ker\big(\overline{\ord}_n\big)=\big(\Laur^{\times}\big)^{n},\qquad
\Laur^{\times}\big/\big(\Laur^{\times}\big)^{n}\;\cong\;\ZZ/n\ZZ,
\]
the isomorphism being induced by pole order mod $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The kernel identification is Theorem~\ref{thm:root} read modulo $n$. Surjectivity of $\overline{\ord}_n$ is witnessed by the monomials $q^k$. The first isomorphism theorem finishes.
\end{proof}

So the pole order mod $n$ is a \emph{complete} invariant of the $n$-th power class and a \emph{sharp} one: every residue occurs. For the Monster-sized product the class is $-194\bmod n$, trivial precisely for the four divisors of $194$.

\subsection{Additive contrast}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:sum}
Let $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ be normalized with $s$ nonempty. Then $\ordt\big(\sum_{i\in s}f_i\big)=-1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
All coefficients in degrees $<-1$ vanish termwise. In degree $-1$ the coefficients sum to $|s|\cdot1\ne0$ in $\CC$.
\end{proof}

The sum of the $194$ normalized series has a \emph{simple} pole, whereas their product has a pole of order $194$. Pole-order growth is purely multiplicative; this is exactly why the obstruction is a group homomorphism and admits no additive counterpart.

\section{Rigidity: the pole certifies its factors}\label{sec:rigid}

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity]\label{thm:rigid}
Let $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ be nonzero Laurent series with $\ord(f_i)\ge-1$ for all $i$, and suppose $\ord\big(\prod_{i\in s}f_i\big)=-|s|$. Then $\ord(f_i)=-1$ for every $i\in s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Additivity gives $\sum_{i\in s}\ord(f_i)=-|s|$. Setting $\varepsilon_i=\ord(f_i)+1\ge0$ yields $\sum_i\varepsilon_i=0$ with all $\varepsilon_i\ge0$, hence $\varepsilon_i=0$ for all $i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $T_1,\dots,T_{194}$ are nonzero with at most simple poles and $\prod_iT_i$ has a pole of order $194$, then each $T_i$ has a pole of order exactly $1$. A Monster-sized pole certifies that all $194$ factors are genuinely singular: no cancellation, and no regular factor.
\end{corollary}

\section{The linear face: the pole filtration and a dimension count}\label{sec:filt}

\begin{definition}[Pole filtration]\label{def:filt}
For $m\ge0$ set $\Pol_m=\{x\in\Laur:\ x_n=0\text{ for all }n<-m\}$.
\end{definition}

Each $\Pol_m$ is a $\CC$-subspace, $\Pol_0=\Pow$, and $\Pol_m\subseteq\Pol_k$ for $m\le k$.

\begin{proposition}[Filtration equals valuation]\label{prop:filtval}
$x\in\Pol_m$ if and only if $\ordt(x)\ge-m$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Leftarrow$) Coefficients strictly below $\ordt$ vanish. ($\Rightarrow$) For $x\ne0$, if $\ord(x)<-m$ then the coefficient at $\ord(x)$ would vanish, contradicting the definition of the order.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Multiplicativity]\label{prop:filtmul}
$\Pol_a\cdot\Pol_b\subseteq\Pol_{a+b}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Immediate from Proposition~\ref{prop:filtval} and additivity of the valuation.
\end{proof}

Two immediate consequences of Propositions~\ref{prop:filtval} and Theorem~\ref{thm:pole}: a normalized series lies in $\Pol_1$, and a product of $m$ normalized series lies in $\Pol_m$ --- the linear form of the pole-order obstruction.

\subsection{Principal parts}

\begin{definition}\label{def:pp}
For $m\ge0$ the \emph{principal part map} is the linear map $\pp_m:\Laur\to\CC^m$, $\pp_m(x)=(x_{-1},x_{-2},\dots,x_{-m})$, and the \emph{principal-part lift} is the linear map
\[
L_m:\CC^m\to\Laur,\qquad L_m(c_0,\dots,c_{m-1})=c_0q^{-1}+c_1q^{-2}+\cdots+c_{m-1}q^{-m}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pp}
$L_m(\CC^m)\subseteq\Pol_m$ and $\pp_m\circ L_m=\mathrm{id}_{\CC^m}$. Moreover, if $x\in\Pol_m$ then $x-L_m(\pp_m(x))\in\Pol_0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The lift is a finite sum of monomials $q^{-(i+1)}$ with $1\le i+1\le m$, none of degree $<-m$. Reading the coefficient of $q^{-(j+1)}$ in $L_m(c)$ picks out $c_j$. For the last claim, in a degree $n<0$ either $n<-m$, where both terms vanish, or $-m\le n\le-1$, where the two coefficients agree by the section identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{space of principal parts of pole order at most $m$} is $\PP_m$, the image of $\Pol_m$ in $\Laur/\Pol_0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Principal-part isomorphism]\label{thm:ppiso}
For every $m\ge0$ the composite $\CC^m\xrightarrow{L_m}\Pol_m\twoheadrightarrow\PP_m$ is a $\CC$-linear isomorphism
\[
\CC^m\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\PP_m,\qquad (c_0,\dots,c_{m-1})\longmapsto\big[c_0q^{-1}+\cdots+c_{m-1}q^{-m}\big].
\]
Consequently $\dim_{\CC}\PP_m=m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
\emph{Injectivity:} if $L_m(c)\in\Pol_0$ then all negative coefficients vanish, and the coefficient at $-(j+1)$ is $c_j$, so $c=0$. \emph{Surjectivity:} for $x\in\Pol_m$, Lemma~\ref{lem:pp} gives $x\equiv L_m(\pp_m(x))\pmod{\Pol_0}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Graded pieces]\label{thm:graded}
For every $m\ge0$ the quotient $\Pol_{m+1}/\Pol_m$ is one-dimensional over $\CC$, spanned by the class of $q^{-(m+1)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The map $\CC\to\Pol_{m+1}/\Pol_m$, $c\mapsto[c\,q^{-(m+1)}]$, is well defined. It is injective: if $c\,q^{-(m+1)}\in\Pol_m$ then reading degree $-(m+1)<-m$ gives $c=0$. It is surjective: for $x\in\Pol_{m+1}$ the difference $x-x_{-(m+1)}q^{-(m+1)}$ lies in $\Pol_m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Riemann--Roch shadow]
Theorems~\ref{thm:ppiso} and \ref{thm:graded} are the formal-Laurent instance of the classical count $\ell(D)-\ell(D-P)\le1$ for divisors supported at a single point. In the local formal setting the inequality is \emph{always} an equality: the filtration jumps by exactly one dimension per unit of pole order, because the residue field is $\CC$ itself. Conceptually, the pole-order obstruction of a product of $m$ normalized series is not merely the integer $m$; it is a \emph{vector} in an $m$-dimensional space, and the order records the position of that vector in the filtration.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Locating the Monster-sized product}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:monsterfilt}
Let $P=\prod_{i=1}^{194}\mathcal T(c_i)$ for arbitrary tails. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item $P\in\Pol_{194}$ and $P\notin\Pol_{193}$;
\item $P_{-194}=1$, i.e.\ the deepest coordinate of $\pp_{194}(P)$ equals $1$;
\item $\dim_{\CC}\PP_{194}=194$, and the class of $P$ in $\Laur/\Pol_0$ is nonzero.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:pole}, $\ord(P)=-194$ with leading coefficient $1$; Proposition~\ref{prop:filtval} gives (1) upward and (2). If $P\in\Pol_{193}$ then the coefficient at $-194<-193$ would vanish, contradicting (2). Part (3) is Theorem~\ref{thm:ppiso} plus the observation that $P\in\Pol_0$ would again force $P_{-194}=0$.
\end{proof}

Thus the Monster-sized product occupies the \emph{top} graded piece of the filtration exactly.

\section{The combinatorial face: coefficients as symmetric functions}\label{sec:comb}

\begin{theorem}[Master coefficient identity]\label{thm:master}
Let $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ be normalized with $m=|s|$. Then for every $k\ge0$,
\[
\Big(\prod_{i\in s}f_i\Big)_{\,k-m}=\Big(\prod_{i\in s}\widehat{f_i}\Big)_{\,k},
\]
the right-hand side being a power-series coefficient of the corrected product.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Corollary~\ref{cor:fact}, $\prod_if_i=q^{-m}U$ with $U=\prod_i\widehat{f_i}$, and multiplication by $q^{-m}$ shifts every coefficient index down by $m$.
\end{proof}

Every Laurent coefficient of a normalized product is therefore a power-series coefficient of a normalized object: the pole is a pure shift.

\begin{definition}
For $a\in\CC$ set $\ell(a):=q^{-1}+a$, the \emph{linear} normalized series with tail $(a,0,0,\dots)$; its corrected part is $\widehat{\ell(a)}=1+aq$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:esym}
$\displaystyle\Big(\prod_{i\in s}(1+a_iq)\Big)_{\,k}=\sum_{t\subseteq s,\,|t|=k}\prod_{i\in t}a_i=e_k(a)$, the $k$-th elementary symmetric function.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Expand by choosing, for each $i$, either $1$ or $a_iq$; a choice set $t$ contributes $\big(\prod_{i\in t}a_i\big)q^{|t|}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Closed formula]\label{thm:closed}
For $a:s\to\CC$ with $m=|s|$ and every $k\ge0$,
\[
\Big(\prod_{i\in s}\big(q^{-1}+a_i\big)\Big)_{\,k-m}=e_k\big((a_i)_{i\in s}\big),
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\prod_{i\in s}\big(q^{-1}+a_i\big)=\sum_{k=0}^{m}e_k(a)\,q^{\,k-m}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:master} with Lemma~\ref{lem:esym}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Support and endpoints]
The product is supported in degrees $-m,\dots,0$; the deepest coefficient (degree $-m$) is $e_0=1$; and the constant coefficient (degree $0$) is $e_m(a)=\prod_{i\in s}a_i$, a Vieta relation.
\end{corollary}

\begin{example}
$(q^{-1}+2)(q^{-1}+3)=q^{-2}+5q^{-1}+6$, and indeed $e_1(2,3)=5$ sits in degree $1-2=-1$. Likewise $(q^{-1}+2)(q^{-1}+3)(q^{-1}+5)=q^{-3}+10q^{-2}+31q^{-1}+30$, with $e_2(2,3,5)=6+10+15=31$ in degree $2-3=-1$.
\end{example}

\begin{corollary}[Monster instance]
For $a_1,\dots,a_{194}\in\CC$, the product $\prod_{i=1}^{194}(q^{-1}+a_i)$ has coefficient $e_k(a)$ in degree $k-194$; its deepest coefficient is $1$ and its constant coefficient is $\prod_{i=1}^{194}a_i$. Its Laurent expansion is the finite sum $\sum_{k=0}^{194}e_k(a)q^{k-194}$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Moving the obstruction: replication}\label{sec:repl}

\begin{definition}[Replication operator]
For $d\ge1$, let $V_d:\Laur\to\Laur$ be the substitution $q\mapsto q^d$, induced by the order-embedding $k\mapsto dk$ of the exponent group $\ZZ$. It is an injective ring homomorphism.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:replord}
$\ordt(V_dx)=d\cdot\ordt(x)$ for all $x$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$V_d$ relabels exponents by the increasing injection $k\mapsto dk$, so the least exponent of the support maps to the least exponent of the image.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Root spectrum after replication]\label{thm:replspec}
For normalized $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ with $m=|s|$ and $d,n\ge1$,
\[
\exists\,y\in\Laur:\ y^n=V_d\Big(\prod_{i\in s}f_i\Big)\iff n\mid dm.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:root} to $V_d\prod_if_i$, whose order is $-dm$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:pole} and Proposition~\ref{prop:replord}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Monster after replication]\label{cor:replmonster}
$V_d\big(\prod_{i=1}^{194}\mathcal T(c_i)\big)$ has an $n$-th root if and only if $n\mid194d$. In particular the \emph{third} replication is a perfect cube, even though the original product is not; every replication is a perfect square; and the fifth root remains obstructed at depth $3$, since $5\nmid582$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Minimal replication depth]\label{thm:depth}
For $n,d\ge1$,
\[
\exists\,y:\ y^n=V_d\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{194}\mathcal T(c_i)\Big)\iff \frac{n}{\gcd(n,194)}\ \Big|\ d,
\]
so $n/\gcd(n,194)$ is the minimal depth at which an $n$-th root appears.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:replspec} the condition is $n\mid194d$. Write $g=\gcd(n,194)$, $n=ga$, $194=gb$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$. Then $n\mid194d\iff a\mid bd\iff a\mid d$ by coprimality, and $a=n/g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
$3/\gcd(3,194)=3$: a cube root first appears at depth $3$. $4/\gcd(4,194)=2$: a fourth root already appears at depth $2$, because $2\mid194$ does half the work. $5/\gcd(5,194)=5$: a fifth root needs depth $5$.
\end{example}

\section{Dissolving the obstruction: divisible value groups}\label{sec:puiseux}

\begin{definition}[Puiseux-type Hahn field]
Let $\Puis$ denote the Hahn series field with value group $\QQ$ and coefficient field $\CC$: formal sums $y=\sum_{r\in\QQ}y_rq^r$ whose support $\{r:y_r\ne0\}$ is well ordered. Order, leading coefficient and additivity of the valuation are defined as before, now with values in $\QQ$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Exponent extension]
The map $\iota:\Laur\to\Puis$ induced by the inclusion $\ZZ\hookrightarrow\QQ$ of value groups is an injective ring homomorphism preserving order.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Dissolution]\label{thm:dissolve}
Let $(f_i)_{i\in s}$ be normalized with $m=|s|$ and let $n\ge1$. There exists $y\in\Puis$ with $y^n=\iota\big(\prod_{i\in s}f_i\big)$; explicitly $y=q^{-m/n}\cdot\iota(w)$, where $w\in\Pow$ is the binomial $n$-th root of the corrected product $U=\prod_i\widehat{f_i}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Proposition~\ref{prop:binom} supplies $w$ with $w^n=U$ and $w(0)=1$; then $y^n=q^{-m}\iota(U)=\iota\big(\prod_if_i\big)$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:fact}. The exponent $-m/n$ is a legitimate element of $\QQ$; this is the only step that fails over $\ZZ$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The Monster is a $194$-th power of a simple-pole series]\label{thm:194root}
For arbitrary tails there exists $y\in\Puis$ with
\[
y^{194}=\iota\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{194}\mathcal T(c_i)\Big)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \ordt(y)=-1.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Take $y=q^{-1}\iota(w)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:dissolve} with $n=m=194$; the order is $-1+0=-1$ since $\iota(w)$ has order $0$.
\end{proof}

The $194$-fold pole is thus literally $194$ copies of one simple pole. Over $\QQ$-exponents every $n\ge1$ works, in sharp contrast with the $\ZZ$-graded answer $n\mid194$: the obstruction is a property of the value group $\ZZ$, not of the series.

\section{Interpolation: one hierarchy, two costumes}\label{sec:interp}

\begin{definition}
For $N\ge1$ let $\tfrac1N\ZZ=\{k/N:k\in\ZZ\}\subseteq\QQ$, a subgroup containing $\ZZ$ and closed under addition.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Support criterion, sharpest form]\label{thm:support}
Let $S\subseteq\QQ$ contain every integer and be closed under addition. Let $P=\prod_{i=1}^{194}\mathcal T(c_i)$ and $n\ge1$. Then
\[
\Big(\exists\,y\in\Puis:\ y^n=\iota(P)\ \text{and}\ \supp(y)\subseteq S\Big)\iff \frac{-194}{n}\in S.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) Such a $y$ is nonzero and $n\ord(y)=-194$, so $\ord(y)=-194/n$; the order always lies in the support. ($\Leftarrow$) Take $y=q^{-194/n}\iota(w)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:dissolve}. Its support lies in $\{-194/n\}+\supp(\iota w)$ with $\supp(\iota w)\subseteq\ZZ\subseteq S$; closure under addition gives $\supp(y)\subseteq S$.
\end{proof}

The existence of an $n$-th root is decided by the membership of a \emph{single rational number} in the exponent set --- the strongest possible expression of ``the pole order is the complete obstruction''.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:lattice}
For $N,n\ge1$: $-194/n\in\tfrac1N\ZZ$ if and only if $n\mid194N$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$-194/n=k/N$ for some $k\in\ZZ$ iff $-194N=kn$ iff $n\mid194N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Graded interpolation]\label{thm:interp}
For $N,n\ge1$,
\[
\Big(\exists\,y\in\Puis:\ y^n=\iota(P),\ \supp(y)\subseteq\tfrac1N\ZZ\Big)\iff n\mid194N.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:support} with $S=\tfrac1N\ZZ$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:lattice}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Value-group refinement equals replication depth]\label{thm:same}
For $N,n\ge1$,
\[
\Big(\exists\,y:\ y^n=\iota(P),\ \supp(y)\subseteq\tfrac1N\ZZ\Big)\iff\Big(\exists\,z\in\Laur:\ z^n=V_N(P)\Big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both sides are equivalent to $n\mid194N$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:interp} and Corollary~\ref{cor:replmonster} respectively.
\end{proof}

Setting $N=1$ recovers the $\ZZ$-graded spectrum $n\mid194$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:monster}; letting $N$ absorb any denominator recovers the unobstructed $\QQ$-graded answer of Theorem~\ref{thm:dissolve}.

\begin{corollary}
A cube root of $P$ exists with exponents in $\tfrac1N\ZZ$ if and only if $3\mid N$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:interp} the condition is $3\mid194N$; since $\gcd(3,194)=1$ this is $3\mid N$.
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithms}

The theory is entirely effective.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Algorithm A (Root spectrum).} \emph{Input:} $m\ge1$, bound $B$. \emph{Output:} the set of $n\le B$ for which the product of $m$ normalized series has an $n$-th root. \emph{Method:} return the divisors of $m$ up to $B$. \emph{Correctness:} Corollary~\ref{cor:specnorm}. \emph{Complexity:} $O(\sqrt m)$ by trial division.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Algorithm B (Minimal replication depth).} \emph{Input:} $n,m\ge1$. \emph{Output:} the least $d\ge1$ with an $n$-th root after $V_d$. \emph{Method:} return $n/\gcd(n,m)$. \emph{Correctness:} Theorem~\ref{thm:depth}. \emph{Complexity:} $O(\log\min(n,m))$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Algorithm C (Explicit root construction).} \emph{Input:} the tails of $m$ normalized series, an exponent $n$, a truncation order $K$. \emph{Output:} the first $K$ terms of an $n$-th root over $\QQ$-exponents. \emph{Method:} form the truncated corrected product $U=\prod_i\widehat{f_i}$; set $a=U-1$ and compute $w=\sum_{k\le K}\binom{1/n}{k}a^k$, legitimate because $a$ has zero constant term so $a^k=O(q^k)$; return $\big(-m/n,\,w\big)$ representing $y=q^{-m/n}w$. \emph{Correctness:} Theorem~\ref{thm:dissolve}. \emph{Complexity:} $O(K^2)$ coefficient operations plus $O(mK)$ for the product. When $n\mid m$ the exponent is an integer and the same $w$ produces a genuine element of $\Laur$.

\section{Applications and interpretation}

\emph{A closed-form coefficient calculus.} Theorem~\ref{thm:master} says the entire Laurent expansion of a normalized product is a shifted power-series expansion; with Theorem~\ref{thm:closed} this converts questions about deep coefficients into questions about symmetric functions of the tails.

\emph{A sharp certificate of singularity.} Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid} turns the pole-order theorem into a diagnostic: observing a pole of order $m$ in a product of $m$ at-most-simple-pole factors \emph{proves} that every factor is singular. Where one has access to the product but not the factors, the order of the pole is a complete certificate against cancellation.

\emph{A model of obstruction theory.} An existence question governed by the triviality of a class in a discrete group is a recurring pattern. What is unusual here is that the pattern is realized exactly: the invariant is complete (Theorem~\ref{thm:classes}), sharp, and one can deform the ambient value group and watch the obstruction respond according to a formula (Theorems~\ref{thm:replspec}, \ref{thm:dissolve}, \ref{thm:interp}).

\emph{Filtrations and dimension counts.} Theorems~\ref{thm:ppiso} and \ref{thm:graded} identify the linear structure underlying the invariant: the pole order is the position of a vector in a filtration whose graded pieces are each one-dimensional, the local formal analogue of the Riemann--Roch count at a point.

\section{Discussion}

\emph{The results are universal in the tails.} No coefficient beyond the residue is used anywhere. The moonshine instance is a specialization; the phenomena are consequences of shape and of the value group, not of the deep arithmetic determining the McKay--Thompson coefficients. Conversely, the pole order cannot detect moonshine-specific structure: it is a coarse but perfectly rigid invariant.

\emph{The hypotheses on the coefficient field are exactly what is used.} Characteristic zero enters through the binomial coefficients $\binom{1/n}{k}$, algebraic closedness through the extraction of $n$-th roots of constants. Over a field failing either, the power-series factor of the splitting would contribute its own obstruction and Theorem~\ref{thm:root} would acquire a second condition. That the answer over $\CC$ is purely arithmetic is a statement about $\CC$ as much as about $q$.

\emph{Multiplicativity is essential.} Proposition~\ref{prop:sum} makes the point sharply: the same $194$ series, added rather than multiplied, produce a simple pole. All of the structure above depends on additivity of the valuation under multiplication.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item \textbf{Beyond squarefree $m$.} The class count $194=2\cdot97$ is squarefree, which is why the root spectrum is small and the fourth root fails. For general $m$ with repeated prime factors the interaction between the multiplicity structure of $m$ and the minimal replication depth $n/\gcd(n,m)$ deserves systematic treatment as a statement about the divisor lattice.
\item \textbf{General value groups.} Theorem~\ref{thm:support} is stated for additively closed subsets of $\QQ$ containing $\ZZ$. The natural generality is a Hahn field over an arbitrary ordered abelian group $\Gamma\supseteq\ZZ$, with criterion ``$-m/n$ exists in $\Gamma$'', recovering Theorem~\ref{thm:dissolve} when $\Gamma$ is divisible and Theorem~\ref{thm:root} when $\Gamma=\ZZ$. Quantifying the failure by $\Gamma/n\Gamma$ would refine Theorem~\ref{thm:classes}.
\item \textbf{Positive characteristic and non-closed coefficient fields.} Over characteristic $p$, $p$-th roots interact with the Frobenius and Proposition~\ref{prop:binom} fails; over a non-closed field $k$ the constant term contributes a class in $k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{n}$. The expected statement is an exact sequence relating $k((q))^{\times}/(k((q))^{\times})^{n}$ to $\ZZ/n$ and $k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{n}$.
\item \textbf{Higher-order poles and mixed shapes.} Allowing factors of order $-e_i$ replaces $m$ by $\sum_ie_i$ throughout, but rigidity then acquires partition-theoretic content: which multisets of orders are consistent with a prescribed product order?
\item \textbf{Symmetric-function refinements.} Theorem~\ref{thm:closed} handles linear tails. For general tails, expressing the coefficients of the corrected product in a symmetric or quasi-symmetric basis, and identifying which expressions are forced by the normalized shape alone, would complete the combinatorial face.
\item \textbf{Replication as a Hecke-type action.} The operator used here is the bare substitution $q\mapsto q^d$. Extending Theorem~\ref{thm:replspec} to genuine Hecke operators --- averages over cosets, with additive corrections --- would connect the pole-order calculus to the replication formulas of moonshine proper.
\item \textbf{Effective root computation and stability.} Newton iteration on $w\mapsto w-(w^n-U)/(nw^{n-1})$ would replace the $O(K^2)$ binomial substitution by quadratic convergence in the truncation order; quantifying coefficient growth and numerical conditioning at moonshine scale is open.
\end{enumerate}

The Pole-Order Obstruction — numerical demonstrations.

Self-contained, dependency-free Python (standard library only) illustrating the
main results about products of *normalized* formal Laurent series

        T = q^{-1} + c_0 + c_1 q + c_2 q^2 + ...

over the complex numbers, and in particular the Monster-sized case of m = 194
factors (one per conjugacy class of the Monster simple group).

Results demonstrated
--------------------
1.  Pole-Order Theorem: a product of m normalized series has order exactly -m,
    with leading coefficient 1; multiplying by q^m restores order 0.
2.  Root-Extraction Theorem: a nonzero Laurent series is an n-th power iff
    n divides its order.  For m = 194 the root spectrum is {1, 2, 97, 194}.
3.  Power classes: order mod n is a complete and sharp invariant of the n-th
    power class in the unit group.
4.  Additive contrast: a sum of m normalized series has order -1, not -m.
5.  Rigidity: a pole of order m in a product of m at-most-simple-pole factors
    forces every factor to have a simple pole.
6.  Pole filtration and principal parts: dim PP_m = m, graded pieces are
    1-dimensional, and the Monster-sized product sits in Pol_194 \\ Pol_193
    with deepest coordinate 1.
7.  Elementary symmetric functions: for linear factors q^{-1} + a_i the
    coefficient in degree k - m is e_k(a).
8.  Replication V_d : q -> q^d multiplies order by d; root spectrum becomes the
    divisors of 194 d; minimal depth for an n-th root is n / gcd(n, 194).
9.  Dissolution over Q-exponents: an n-th root exists for every n, built as
    q^{-m/n} times the binomial n-th root of the corrected unit part.
10. Interpolation: an n-th root with exponents in (1/N)Z exists iff n | 194 N,
    the very same criterion as replication at depth N.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

MONSTER_CLASS_COUNT: int = 194


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Truncated Laurent series
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Laurent:
    """A formal Laurent series truncated above a fixed exponent bound.

    Internally a dict from integer exponent to Fraction coefficient, together
    with `top`: coefficients in degrees > top are not tracked.
    """

    __slots__ = ("coeffs", "top")

    def __init__(self, coeffs: Dict[int, Fraction], top: int) -> None:
        self.top: int = top
        self.coeffs: Dict[int, Fraction] = {
            n: Fraction(c) for n, c in coeffs.items() if c != 0 and n <= top
        }

    # -- basic accessors ----------------------------------------------------

    def coeff(self, n: int) -> Fraction:
        return self.coeffs.get(n, Fraction(0))

    def is_zero(self) -> bool:
        return not self.coeffs

    def order(self) -> int:
        """Least exponent with a nonzero coefficient.  Undefined for 0."""
        if self.is_zero():
            raise ValueError("the zero series has no order")
        return min(self.coeffs)

    def leading_coeff(self) -> Fraction:
        return self.coeff(self.order())

    # -- arithmetic ---------------------------------------------------------

    def __add__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        top = min(self.top, other.top)
        out: Dict[int, Fraction] = dict(self.coeffs)
        for n, c in other.coeffs.items():
            out[n] = out.get(n, Fraction(0)) + c
        return Laurent(out, top)

    def __mul__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        if self.is_zero() or other.is_zero():
            return Laurent({}, min(self.top, other.top))
        # Truncation bound: product is reliable up to
        # min(self.top + ord(other), other.top + ord(self)).
        top = min(self.top + other.order(), other.top + self.order())
        out: Dict[int, Fraction] = {}
        for a, ca in self.coeffs.items():
            for b, cb in other.coeffs.items():
                if a + b <= top:
                    out[a + b] = out.get(a + b, Fraction(0)) + ca * cb
        return Laurent(out, top)

    def __pow__(self, n: int) -> "Laurent":
        result = Laurent({0: Fraction(1)}, self.top - self.order() * max(n - 1, 0))
        for _ in range(n):
            result = result * self
        return result

    def shift(self, k: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Multiply by q^k."""
        return Laurent({n + k: c for n, c in self.coeffs.items()}, self.top + k)

    def replicate(self, d: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Apply V_d : q -> q^d."""
        return Laurent({n * d: c for n, c in self.coeffs.items()}, self.top * d)

    def truncate(self, top: int) -> "Laurent":
        return Laurent(dict(self.coeffs), min(self.top, top))

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        if self.is_zero():
            return "0"
        pieces: List[str] = []
        for n in sorted(self.coeffs):
            c = self.coeffs[n]
            cs = str(c)
            if n == 0:
                pieces.append(cs)
            elif n == 1:
                pieces.append(f"{cs}*q")
            else:
                pieces.append(f"{cs}*q^{n}")
        return " + ".join(pieces) + f" + O(q^{self.top + 1})"


def normalized(tail: Sequence[Fraction | int], top: int) -> Laurent:
    """The normalized series q^{-1} + tail[0] + tail[1] q + ... ."""
    coeffs: Dict[int, Fraction] = {-1: Fraction(1)}
    for k, c in enumerate(tail):
        if k <= top:
            coeffs[k] = Fraction(c)
    return Laurent(coeffs, top)


def linear_normalized(a: Fraction | int, top: int) -> Laurent:
    """The linear normalized series q^{-1} + a."""
    return Laurent({-1: Fraction(1), 0: Fraction(a)}, top)


def prod(series: Iterable[Laurent]) -> Laurent:
    it = iter(series)
    result = next(it)
    for s in it:
        result = result * s
    return result


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Arithmetic of the obstruction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def divisors(m: int) -> List[int]:
    out: List[int] = []
    d = 1
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            out.append(d)
            if d != m // d:
                out.append(m // d)
        d += 1
    return sorted(out)


def root_spectrum(m: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Exponents n <= bound for which a product of m normalized series is an
    n-th power in C((q)).  By the Root-Extraction Theorem: the divisors of m."""
    return [n for n in divisors(m) if n <= bound]


def has_root(m: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Does a product of m normalized series have an n-th root in C((q))?"""
    return n >= 1 and m % n == 0


def has_root_after_replication(m: int, n: int, d: int) -> bool:
    """Does V_d of the product have an n-th root?  Criterion: n | d*m."""
    return n >= 1 and d >= 1 and (d * m) % n == 0


def minimal_replication_depth(n: int, m: int = MONSTER_CLASS_COUNT) -> int:
    """Least d with an n-th root after V_d.  Equals n / gcd(n, m)."""
    return n // gcd(n, m)


def has_lattice_root(m: int, n: int, N: int) -> bool:
    """Root with exponents in (1/N)Z inside the Puiseux field: n | m*N."""
    return n >= 1 and N >= 1 and (m * N) % n == 0


def critical_exponent(m: int, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """The single rational number whose membership in the exponent set decides
    the existence of an n-th root: -m/n."""
    return Fraction(-m, n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Symmetric functions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def elementary_symmetric(a: Sequence[Fraction | int], k: int) -> Fraction:
    """e_k(a), computed by the standard O(m*k) dynamic program."""
    e: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (k + 1)
    e[0] = Fraction(1)
    for x in a:
        for j in range(min(k, len(a)), 0, -1):
            e[j] += Fraction(x) * e[j - 1]
    return e[k]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Binomial n-th root of a power series with constant term 1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def binomial_coefficient(r: Fraction, k: int) -> Fraction:
    """The generalized binomial coefficient C(r, k) for rational r."""
    num = Fraction(1)
    for j in range(k):
        num *= (r - j)
    den = Fraction(1)
    for j in range(1, k + 1):
        den *= j
    return num / den


def power_series_nth_root(u: List[Fraction], n: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Given u = [u_0, ..., u_K] with u_0 = 1, return w with w_0 = 1 and
    w^n = u to order K.

    Degree-by-degree recursion: suppose w_0, ..., w_{k-1} are known and w_k is
    provisionally 0.  In the expansion of w^n, the coefficient of q^k depends on
    w_k only through the single linear term n * w_0^{n-1} * w_k = n * w_k.
    Hence setting w_k := (u_k - [q^k](w^n)) / n corrects degree k exactly and
    leaves all lower degrees untouched.  This is the algebraic realisation of
    the binomial series root of Proposition 2.3.
    """
    assert u and u[0] == 1, "constant term must be 1"
    K = len(u) - 1
    w: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    w[0] = Fraction(1)
    for k in range(1, K + 1):
        # Compute the coefficient of q^k in w^n using the current w
        # (with w[k] still 0); the missing contribution is exactly n*w[k].
        cur = _poly_pow(w, n, k)
        w[k] = (u[k] - cur[k]) / n
    return w


def _poly_mul(a: List[Fraction], b: List[Fraction], K: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    out = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai == 0 or i > K:
            continue
        for j, bj in enumerate(b):
            if bj == 0 or i + j > K:
                continue
            out[i + j] += ai * bj
    return out


def _poly_pow(a: List[Fraction], n: int, K: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    out = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    out[0] = Fraction(1)
    for _ in range(n):
        out = _poly_mul(out, a, K)
    return out


def puiseux_root_of_normalized_product(
    tails: Sequence[Sequence[Fraction | int]], n: int, K: int
) -> Tuple[Fraction, List[Fraction]]:
    """The n-th root, over Q-exponents, of a product of m normalized series.

    Returns (e, w) representing y = q^e * (w_0 + w_1 q + ... ), with e = -m/n
    and w^n equal to the corrected product q^m * prod(T_i) to order K.
    """
    m = len(tails)
    # corrected part of q^{-1} + c_0 + c_1 q + ... is 1 + c_0 q + c_1 q^2 + ...
    u: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * K
    for tail in tails:
        f: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * K
        for k, c in enumerate(tail):
            if k + 1 <= K:
                f[k + 1] = Fraction(c)
        u = _poly_mul(u, f, K)
    w = power_series_nth_root(u, n)
    return Fraction(-m, n), w

def demo_pole_order() -> None:

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

MONSTER_CLASS_COUNT: int = 194


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Truncated Laurent series
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Laurent:
    """A formal Laurent series truncated above a fixed exponent bound.

    Internally a dict from integer exponent to Fraction coefficient, together
    with `top`: coefficients in degrees > top are not tracked.
    """

    __slots__ = ("coeffs", "top")

    def __init__(self, coeffs: Dict[int, Fraction], top: int) -> None:
        self.top: int = top
        self.coeffs: Dict[int, Fraction] = {
            n: Fraction(c) for n, c in coeffs.items() if c != 0 and n <= top
        }

    # -- basic accessors ----------------------------------------------------

    def coeff(self, n: int) -> Fraction:
        return self.coeffs.get(n, Fraction(0))

    def is_zero(self) -> bool:
        return not self.coeffs

    def order(self) -> int:
        """Least exponent with a nonzero coefficient.  Undefined for 0."""
        if self.is_zero():
            raise ValueError("the zero series has no order")
        return min(self.coeffs)

    def leading_coeff(self) -> Fraction:
        return self.coeff(self.order())

    # -- arithmetic ---------------------------------------------------------

    def __add__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        top = min(self.top, other.top)
        out: Dict[int, Fraction] = dict(self.coeffs)
        for n, c in other.coeffs.items():
            out[n] = out.get(n, Fraction(0)) + c
        return Laurent(out, top)

    def __mul__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        if self.is_zero() or other.is_zero():
            return Laurent({}, min(self.top, other.top))
        # Truncation bound: product is reliable up to
        # min(self.top + ord(other), other.top + ord(self)).
        top = min(self.top + other.order(), other.top + self.order())
        out: Dict[int, Fraction] = {}
        for a, ca in self.coeffs.items():
            for b, cb in other.coeffs.items():
                if a + b <= top:
                    out[a + b] = out.get(a + b, Fraction(0)) + ca * cb
        return Laurent(out, top)

    def __pow__(self, n: int) -> "Laurent":
        result = Laurent({0: Fraction(1)}, self.top - self.order() * max(n - 1, 0))
        for _ in range(n):
            result = result * self
        return result

    def shift(self, k: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Multiply by q^k."""
        return Laurent({n + k: c for n, c in self.coeffs.items()}, self.top + k)

    def replicate(self, d: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Apply V_d : q -> q^d."""
        return Laurent({n * d: c for n, c in self.coeffs.items()}, self.top * d)

    def truncate(self, top: int) -> "Laurent":
        return Laurent(dict(self.coeffs), min(self.top, top))

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        if self.is_zero():
            return "0"
        pieces: List[str] = []
        for n in sorted(self.coeffs):
            c = self.coeffs[n]
            cs = str(c)
            if n == 0:
                pieces.append(cs)
            elif n == 1:
                pieces.append(f"{cs}*q")
            else:
                pieces.append(f"{cs}*q^{n}")
        return " + ".join(pieces) + f" + O(q^{self.top + 1})"


def normalized(tail: Sequence[Fraction | int], top: int) -> Laurent:
    """The normalized series q^{-1} + tail[0] + tail[1] q + ... ."""
    coeffs: Dict[int, Fraction] = {-1: Fraction(1)}
    for k, c in enumerate(tail):
        if k <= top:
            coeffs[k] = Fraction(c)
    return Laurent(coeffs, top)


def linear_normalized(a: Fraction | int, top: int) -> Laurent:
    """The linear normalized series q^{-1} + a."""
    return Laurent({-1: Fraction(1), 0: Fraction(a)}, top)


def prod(series: Iterable[Laurent]) -> Laurent:
    it = iter(series)
    result = next(it)
    for s in it:
        result = result * s
    return result


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Arithmetic of the obstruction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def divisors(m: int) -> List[int]:
    out: List[int] = []
    d = 1
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            out.append(d)
            if d != m // d:
                out.append(m // d)
        d += 1
    return sorted(out)


def root_spectrum(m: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Exponents n <= bound for which a product of m normalized series is an
    n-th power in C((q)).  By the Root-Extraction Theorem: the divisors of m."""
    return [n for n in divisors(m) if n <= bound]


def has_root(m: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Does a product of m normalized series have an n-th root in C((q))?"""
    return n >= 1 and m % n == 0


def has_root_after_replication(m: int, n: int, d: int) -> bool:
    """Does V_d of the product have an n-th root?  Criterion: n | d*m."""
    return n >= 1 and d >= 1 and (d * m) % n == 0


def minimal_replication_depth(n: int, m: int = MONSTER_CLASS_COUNT) -> int:
    """Least d with an n-th root after V_d.  Equals n / gcd(n, m)."""
    return n // gcd(n, m)


def has_lattice_root(m: int, n: int, N: int) -> bool:
    """Root with exponents in (1/N)Z inside the Puiseux field: n | m*N."""
    return n >= 1 and N >= 1 and (m * N) % n == 0


def critical_exponent(m: int, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """The single rational number whose membership in the exponent set decides
    the existence of an n-th root: -m/n."""
    return Fraction(-m, n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Symmetric functions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def elementary_symmetric(a: Sequence[Fraction | int], k: int) -> Fraction:
    """e_k(a), computed by the standard O(m*k) dynamic program."""
    e: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (k + 1)
    e[0] = Fraction(1)
    for x in a:
        for j in range(min(k, len(a)), 0, -1):
            e[j] += Fraction(x) * e[j - 1]
    return e[k]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Binomial n-th root of a power series with constant term 1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def binomial_coefficient(r: Fraction, k: int) -> Fraction:
    """The generalized binomial coefficient C(r, k) for rational r."""
    num = Fraction(1)
    for j in range(k):
        num *= (r - j)
    den = Fraction(1)
    for j in range(1, k + 1):
        den *= j
    return num / den


def power_series_nth_root(u: List[Fraction], n: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Given u = [u_0, ..., u_K] with u_0 = 1, return w with w_0 = 1 and
    w^n = u to order K.

    Degree-by-degree recursion: suppose w_0, ..., w_{k-1} are known and w_k is
    provisionally 0.  In the expansion of w^n, the coefficient of q^k depends on
    w_k only through the single linear term n * w_0^{n-1} * w_k = n * w_k.
    Hence setting w_k := (u_k - [q^k](w^n)) / n corrects degree k exactly and
    leaves all lower degrees untouched.  This is the algebraic realisation of
    the binomial series root of Proposition 2.3.
    """
    assert u and u[0] == 1, "constant term must be 1"
    K = len(u) - 1
    w: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    w[0] = Fraction(1)
    for k in range(1, K + 1):
        # Compute the coefficient of q^k in w^n using the current w
        # (with w[k] still 0); the missing contribution is exactly n*w[k].
        cur = _poly_pow(w, n, k)
        w[k] = (u[k] - cur[k]) / n
    return w


def _poly_mul(a: List[Fraction], b: List[Fraction], K: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    out = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai == 0 or i > K:
            continue
        for j, bj in enumerate(b):
            if bj == 0 or i + j > K:
                continue
            out[i + j] += ai * bj
    return out


def _poly_pow(a: List[Fraction], n: int, K: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    out = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    out[0] = Fraction(1)
    for _ in range(n):
        out = _poly_mul(out, a, K)
    return out


def puiseux_root_of_normalized_product(
    tails: Sequence[Sequence[Fraction | int]], n: int, K: int
) -> Tuple[Fraction, List[Fraction]]:
    """The n-th root, over Q-exponents, of a product of m normalized series.

    Returns (e, w) representing y = q^e * (w_0 + w_1 q + ... ), with e = -m/n
    and w^n equal to the corrected product q^m * prod(T_i) to order K.
    """
    m = len(tails)
    # corrected part of q^{-1} + c_0 + c_1 q + ... is 1 + c_0 q + c_1 q^2 + ...
    u: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * K
    for tail in tails:
        f: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * K
        for k, c in enumerate(tail):
            if k + 1 <= K:
                f[k + 1] = Fraction(c)
        u = _poly_mul(u, f, K)
    w = power_series_nth_root(u, n)
    return Fraction(-m, n), w

def demo_pole_order() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1.  POLE-ORDER THEOREM:  ord(prod of m normalized series) = -m")
    print("=" * 74)
    top = 6
    tails = [[1, 2, 3], [0, -1, 4], [5, 5, 5], [2, 0, 7], [-3, 1, 1]]
    for m in range(1, len(tails) + 1):
        p = prod(normalized(t, top) for t in tails[:m])
        print(f"  m = {m}:  ord = {p.order():>3}   leading coeff = {p.leading_coeff()}"
              f"   (predicted ord = {-m})")
        assert p.order() == -m and p.leading_coeff() == 1
    p = prod(normalized(t, top) for t in tails)
    corrected = p.shift(len(tails))
    print(f"\n  Multiplying by q^{len(tails)} restores order 0:  "
          f"ord = {corrected.order()}, constant term = {corrected.coeff(0)}")
    assert corrected.order() == 0 and corrected.coeff(0) == 1
    print()

def demo_dissolution() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("9.  DISSOLUTION over Q-exponents:  every n works")
    print("=" * 74)
    K = 6
    tails = [[Fraction(1), Fraction(2)], [Fraction(-1), Fraction(3)],
             [Fraction(4), Fraction(0)]]
    m = len(tails)
    for n in (2, 3, 5, 7):
        e, w = puiseux_root_of_normalized_product(tails, n, K)
        # verify w^n equals the corrected product to order K
        u: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * K
        for tail in tails:
            f = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * K
            for k, c in enumerate(tail):
                if k + 1 <= K:
                    f[k + 1] = Fraction(c)
            u = _poly_mul(u, f, K)
        check = _poly_pow(w, n, K)
        ok = check == u
        head = ", ".join(str(w[i]) for i in range(min(4, K + 1)))
        print(f"    n = {n}:  root exponent e = {e}   w = [{head}, ...]   w^n = U ?  {ok}")
        assert ok and e == Fraction(-m, n)
    print(f"\n    For the Monster-sized product the 194-th root has exponent"
          f" -194/194 = {Fraction(-MONSTER_CLASS_COUNT, MONSTER_CLASS_COUNT)}:")
    print("    a simple-pole series whose 194-th power is the whole product.")
    print()

  * exponents in the lattice (1/N)Z          : n | m*N
  * fully divisible exponents (Puiseux, Q)   : always

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import gcd
from typing import Dict, List


def divisors(m: int) -> List[int]:
    """All positive divisors of m, in increasing order.  O(sqrt(m))."""
    if m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("m must be positive")
    small: List[int] = []
    large: List[int] = []
    d = 1
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            small.append(d)
            if d != m // d:
                large.append(m // d)
        d += 1
    return small + large[::-1]


def critical_exponent(m: int, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """The rational number -m/n whose membership in the exponent set decides
    the existence of an n-th root."""
    return Fraction(-m, n)


def root_spectrum_integer(m: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Exponents n <= bound admitting an n-th root over integer exponents."""
    return [n for n in divisors(m) if n <= bound]


def root_spectrum_replicated(m: int, d: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Exponents n <= bound admitting an n-th root after replication V_d."""
    return [n for n in divisors(d * m) if n <= bound]


def root_spectrum_lattice(m: int, N: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Exponents n <= bound admitting an n-th root with exponents in (1/N)Z.
    Identical to the replicated spectrum at depth N."""
    return root_spectrum_replicated(m, N, bound)


def minimal_replication_depth(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Least d >= 1 with n | d*m, namely n / gcd(n, m).  O(log min(n,m))."""
    if n <= 0 or m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("n and m must be positive")
    return n // gcd(n, m)


def spectrum_report(m: int, bound: int, depths: List[int]) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Assemble a full report of the root spectra at several depths."""
    report: Dict[str, object] = {
        "m": m,
        "integer_spectrum": root_spectrum_integer(m, bound),
        "critical_exponents": {n: str(critical_exponent(m, n)) for n in range(1, bound + 1)},
        "minimal_depths": {n: minimal_replication_depth(n, m) for n in range(1, bound + 1)},
        "replicated_spectra": {d: root_spectrum_replicated(m, d, bound) for d in depths},
        "puiseux_spectrum": "every n >= 1",
    }
    return report

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Poly = List[Fraction]


def poly_mul(a: Poly, b: Poly, K: int) -> Poly:
    """Truncated product of two power series, modulo q^{K+1}."""
    out: Poly = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai == 0 or i > K:
            continue
        for j, bj in enumerate(b):
            if bj == 0 or i + j > K:
                continue
            out[i + j] += ai * bj
    return out


def poly_pow(a: Poly, n: int, K: int) -> Poly:
    """Truncated n-th power by binary exponentiation, modulo q^{K+1}."""
    result: Poly = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    result[0] = Fraction(1)
    base = list(a)
    e = n
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:
            result = poly_mul(result, base, K)
        base = poly_mul(base, base, K)
        e >>= 1
    return result


def corrected_product(tails: Sequence[Sequence[Fraction | int]], K: int) -> Poly:
    """U = prod_i (1 + c_{i,0} q + c_{i,1} q^2 + ...), truncated at order K."""
    u: Poly = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    u[0] = Fraction(1)
    for tail in tails:

        f[0] = Fraction(1)
        for k, c in enumerate(tail):
            if k + 1 <= K:
                f[k + 1] = Fraction(c)
        u = poly_mul(u, f, K)
    return u


def nth_root_unit_series(u: Poly, n: int, K: int) -> Poly:
    """The unique w with w_0 = 1 and w^n = u modulo q^{K+1}.

    Degree-by-degree correction: with w_0, ..., w_{k-1} fixed and w_k = 0, the
    coefficient of q^k in w^n depends on w_k only through the linear term
    n * w_0^{n-1} * w_k = n * w_k.  Setting w_k := (u_k - [q^k] w^n) / n
    therefore repairs degree k without disturbing lower degrees.

    if not u or u[0] != 1:
        raise ValueError("the series must have constant term 1")
    w: Poly = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    w[0] = Fraction(1)
    for k in range(1, K + 1):
        current = poly_pow(w, n, k)
        w[k] = (u[k] - current[k]) / n
    return w


def construct_root(
    tails: Sequence[Sequence[Fraction | int]], n: int, K: int
) -> Tuple[Fraction, Poly]:
    """Return (e, w) with y = q^e * w satisfying y^n = prod of the normalized
    series, to truncation order K.  Here e = -m/n."""
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("n must be positive")
    m = len(tails)
    u = corrected_product(tails, K)
    w = nth_root_unit_series(u, n, K)
    return Fraction(-m, n), w

    """Check that the constructed root really is an n-th root, to order K."""
    e, w = construct_root(tails, n, K)
    u = corrected_product(tails, K)
    return poly_pow(w, n, K) == u and e == Fraction(-len(tails), n)

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence

Poly = List[Fraction]


def elementary_symmetric_all(a: Sequence[Fraction | int]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """All elementary symmetric functions [e_0, e_1, ..., e_m] of a, in O(m^2)."""

    for x in a:

    """The full Laurent expansion of prod_i (q^{-1} + a_i), returned as the list

    return elementary_symmetric_all(a)

    """Truncated corrected product U = prod_i (1 + c_{i,0} q + c_{i,1} q^2 + ...)."""
    u: Poly = [Fraction(0)] * (K + 1)
    u[0] = Fraction(1)
    for tail in tails:

        f[0] = Fraction(1)
        for k, c in enumerate(tail):

        for i, ui in enumerate(u):
            if ui == 0:

            for j, fj in enumerate(f):
                if fj == 0 or i + j > K:

      "title": "The Pole-Order Obstruction Explorer",
      "description": "A single, self-contained interactive laboratory for the entire theory. Three sliders control the number of normalized factors m (with a one-click preset at the Monster's 194), the root exponent n, and the lattice refinement / replication depth N. Everything else updates live: the order of the product, the critical exponent -m/n as a reduced fraction, the power class -m mod n, the minimal replication depth n/gcd(n,m), and the dimension of the principal-part space. Four side-by-side verdict panels answer the same question in four ambient settings — integer exponents, after replication q -> q^N, with exponents in the lattice (1/N)Z, and over a fully divisible exponent group — each showing the divisibility criterion that produced it; the second and third panels are always in agreement, which is the interpolation theorem made visible. A number-line canvas draws the exponent lattice as tick marks and places the critical exponent on it, so the reader sees literally that a root exists precisely when the marker lands on a tick. A ladder canvas draws the pole filtration with the product placed on the top rung, in Pol_m and not Pol_{m-1}. A live coefficient calculator lets the reader type constants a_1, a_2, ... and watch the product of linear normalized factors expand into elementary symmetric functions degree by degree. Finally an interpolation heat map over (N, n) lights every cell where n divides mN, with the current selection outlined, showing the whole hierarchy from the bare integer spectrum on the left edge to full dissolution as N grows.",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>The Pole-Order Obstruction Explorer</title>
<style>
  :root{
    --bg:#0f1420; --panel:#182033; --panel2:#1e2740; --ink:#e8edf7; --muted:#9aa8c4;
    --good:#38d39f; --bad:#ff6b81; --accent:#7aa2f7; --warm:#f2b134; --line:#2b3855;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:linear-gradient(160deg,#0f1420,#131b2c 60%,#0f1420);
       color:var(--ink);font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;
       line-height:1.55;padding:26px}
  .wrap{max-width:1120px;margin:0 auto}
  h1{font-size:26px;margin:0 0 4px;letter-spacing:.2px}
  h2{font-size:17px;margin:0 0 10px;color:var(--accent);letter-spacing:.3px}
  .sub{color:var(--muted);margin:0 0 22px;font-size:14.5px}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px;padding:18px 20px;margin-bottom:18px;
         box-shadow:0 6px 24px rgba(0,0,0,.28)}
  .grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:18px}
  @media(max-width:880px){.grid{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
  label{display:block;font-size:13px;color:var(--muted);margin-bottom:5px;letter-spacing:.3px}
  .ctl{margin-bottom:16px}
  input[type=range]{width:100%;accent-color:var(--accent)}
  .val{font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;color:var(--ink);font-weight:600}
  .chipset{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;margin-top:8px}
  .chip{background:var(--panel2);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:999px;padding:4px 12px;font-size:12.5px;
        cursor:pointer;color:var(--muted);transition:.15s}
  .chip:hover{border-color:var(--accent);color:var(--ink)}
  .verdict{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:12px;background:var(--panel2);border-radius:11px;padding:12px 14px;
           margin-bottom:10px;border-left:5px solid var(--line)}
  .verdict.yes{border-left-color:var(--good)}
  .verdict.no{border-left-color:var(--bad)}
  .verdict .badge{font-size:11.5px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.7px;padding:3px 9px;border-radius:6px;white-space:nowrap}
  .verdict.yes .badge{background:rgba(56,211,159,.16);color:var(--good)}
  .verdict.no  .badge{background:rgba(255,107,129,.16);color:var(--bad)}
  .verdict .txt{font-size:13.5px}
  .verdict .txt small{display:block;color:var(--muted);font-size:12px;margin-top:2px}
  .mono{font-family:"SF Mono",ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace}
  .big{font-size:30px;font-weight:700;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;letter-spacing:.5px}
  .kv{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;padding:6px 0;border-bottom:1px dashed var(--line);font-size:13.5px}
  .kv:last-child{border-bottom:none}
  .kv span:first-child{color:var(--muted)}
  canvas{width:100%;display:block;border-radius:10px;background:#121a2b;border:1px solid var(--line)}
  table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:12.7px;margin-top:6px}
  th,td{padding:5px 7px;text-align:center;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
  th{color:var(--muted);font-weight:600;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:.4px}
  td.y{color:var(--good);font-weight:700}
  td.n{color:var(--bad)}
  .note{font-size:12.8px;color:var(--muted);margin-top:10px}
  input[type=text]{width:100%;background:#121a2b;border:1px solid var(--line);color:var(--ink);
                   border-radius:8px;padding:9px 11px;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:13px}
  .coeffs{margin-top:12px;overflow-x:auto}
  .formula{background:#121a2b;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:9px;padding:11px 13px;margin-top:10px;
           font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:13px;color:var(--warm);overflow-x:auto;white-space:nowrap}
  footer{color:var(--muted);font-size:12.3px;text-align:center;margin-top:8px}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">

  <h1>The Pole-Order Obstruction Explorer</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    Multiply <span class="val" id="mEcho">194</span> series of the shape
    <span class="mono">q<sup>−1</sup> + c<sub>0</sub> + c<sub>1</sub>q + …</span>
    — each with a simple pole of residue 1 — and the product has a pole of order exactly
    <span class="mono">m</span>. Whether that product has an <span class="mono">n</span>-th root is decided by
    <em>one rational number</em>: the critical exponent <span class="mono">−m/n</span>.
    Move the sliders and watch the obstruction appear, move, and dissolve.
  </p>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>1 · Controls</h2>
    <div class="grid">
      <div>
        <div class="ctl">
          <label>Number of normalized factors   <span class="val mono" id="mLab">m = 194</span></label>
          <input type="range" id="m" min="1" max="240" value="194">
          <div class="chipset">
            <span class="chip" data-m="194">Monster: m = 194</span>
            <span class="chip" data-m="12">m = 12</span>
            <span class="chip" data-m="36">m = 36</span>
            <span class="chip" data-m="97">m = 97</span>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="ctl">
          <label>Root exponent   <span class="val mono" id="nLab">n = 3</span></label>
          <input type="range" id="n" min="1" max="40" value="3">
          <div class="chipset">
            <span class="chip" data-n="2">square root</span>
            <span class="chip" data-n="3">cube root</span>
            <span class="chip" data-n="4">fourth root</span>
            <span class="chip" data-n="97">n = 97</span>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="ctl">
          <label>Lattice refinement / replication depth   <span class="val mono" id="NLab">N = 1</span></label>
          <input type="range" id="N" min="1" max="24" value="1">
          <div class="chipset">
            <span class="chip" data-N="1">N = 1 (integers)</span>
            <span class="chip" data-N="3">N = 3</span>
            <span class="chip" data-N="6">N = 6</span>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div>
        <div class="kv"><span>order of the product</span><span class="mono val" id="ordVal">−194</span></div>
        <div class="kv"><span>critical exponent −m/n</span><span class="mono val" id="critVal">−194/3</span></div>
        <div class="kv"><span>exponent lattice</span><span class="mono val" id="latVal">(1/1)ℤ = ℤ</span></div>
        <div class="kv"><span>power class of the product mod n</span><span class="mono val" id="clsVal">1 mod 3</span></div>
        <div class="kv"><span>minimal replication depth n / gcd(n, m)</span><span class="mono val" id="depthVal">3</span></div>
        <div class="kv"><span>dimension of the principal-part space</span><span class="mono val" id="dimVal">194</span></div>
        <div class="formula" id="factorization">∏ T<sub>i</sub> = q<sup>−194</sup> · U(q),  U(0) = 1</div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>2 · Four verdicts, one invariant</h2>
    <div class="grid">
      <div>
        <div class="verdict" id="v1">
          <span class="badge">—</span>
          <span class="txt"><b>Integer exponents</b> — a root inside the ordinary Laurent field
            <small id="v1s"></small></span>
        </div>
        <div class="verdict" id="v2">
          <span class="badge">—</span>
          <span class="txt"><b>After replication</b> q → q<sup>N</sup>
            <small id="v2s"></small></span>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div>
        <div class="verdict" id="v3">
          <span class="badge">—</span>
          <span class="txt"><b>Exponents in the lattice</b> (1/N)ℤ
            <small id="v3s"></small></span>
        </div>
        <div class="verdict" id="v4">
          <span class="badge">—</span>
          <span class="txt"><b>Fully divisible exponents</b> (all rationals allowed)
            <small id="v4s"></small></span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <p class="note">
      Verdicts 2 and 3 are <em>always identical</em>: refining the exponent lattice by a factor of N and
      replicating to depth N are one and the same invariant. Verdict 4 is always positive — over a
      divisible value group the obstruction cannot exist, because every rational number is n times another.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>3 · Where does the critical exponent land?</h2>
    <canvas id="line" height="150"></canvas>
    <p class="note">
      The tick marks are the exponent lattice (1/N)ℤ. The marker is the critical exponent −m/n,
      which is forced to be the order of any n-th root. A root supported in the lattice exists exactly when
      the marker sits <em>on</em> a tick.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>4 · The pole filtration</h2>
    <canvas id="filt" height="210"></canvas>
    <p class="note">
      Pol<sub>k</sub> is the space of series whose coefficients vanish in all degrees below −k. Each step up
      the ladder adds exactly one dimension — the new monomial q<sup>−(k+1)</sup> — so the space
      of principal parts of pole order at most m is m-dimensional. The product of m normalized series sits in
      Pol<sub>m</sub> and <em>not</em> in Pol<sub>m−1</sub>: it occupies the top rung exactly, with deepest
      coordinate 1.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>5 · Coefficients are elementary symmetric functions</h2>
    <p class="note" style="margin-top:0">
      Take the simplest normalized shapes, the linear ones q<sup>−1</sup> + a. Then the coefficient of the
      product in degree k − m is the k-th elementary symmetric function of the constants. Type your own
      list below.
    </p>
    <label>Constants a<sub>1</sub>, a<sub>2</sub>, … (comma separated)</label>
    <input type="text" id="avals" value="2, 3, 5">
    <div class="formula" id="prodFormula"></div>
    <div class="coeffs"><table id="ctab"></table></div>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>6 · The interpolation grid</h2>
    <canvas id="grid" height="330"></canvas>
    <p class="note">
      Rows are exponents n, columns are lattice refinements (equivalently replication depths) N. A cell is lit
      exactly when n divides m·N. Column N = 1 is the bare integer spectrum — the divisors of m.
      Moving right, the spectrum grows in a completely predictable way, and every row eventually lights up:
      that is dissolution, reached one denominator at a time.
    </p>
  </div>

  <footer>Move any slider — every number, verdict, and picture updates live.</footer>
</div>

<script>
"use strict";

function gcd(a,b){a=Math.abs(a);b=Math.abs(b);while(b){const t=a%b;a=b;b=t;}return a;}
function fracStr(num,den){const g=gcd(num,den)||1;let p=num/g,q=den/g;if(q<0){p=-p;q=-q;}
  return q===1?String(p):(p+"/"+q);}

const el = id => document.getElementById(id);
const mS = el("m"), nS = el("n"), NS = el("N");

function state(){
  return {m:+mS.value, n:+nS.value, N:+NS.value};
}

function setVerdict(id, ok, text){
  const v = el(id);
  v.classList.toggle("yes", ok); v.classList.toggle("no", !ok);
  v.querySelector(".badge").textContent = ok ? "EXISTS" : "OBSTRUCTED";
  el(id+"s").innerHTML = text;
}

/* ---------- number line ---------- */
function drawLine(){
  const {m,n,N} = state();
  const c = el("line"), dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  const W = c.clientWidth, H = 150;
  c.width = W*dpr; c.height = H*dpr;
  const g = c.getContext("2d"); g.scale(dpr,dpr);
  g.clearRect(0,0,W,H);

  const crit = -m/n;
  // window centred on the critical exponent
  const span = Math.max(2.0, 3.5/N*3);
  const lo = crit - span, hi = crit + span;
  const X = t => 40 + (t-lo)/(hi-lo)*(W-80);

  g.strokeStyle="#2b3855"; g.lineWidth=2;
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(30,H/2); g.lineTo(W-30,H/2); g.stroke();

  // integer ticks (bold) and lattice ticks
  const kmin = Math.ceil(lo*N), kmax = Math.floor(hi*N);
  const maxTicks = 260;
  if (kmax-kmin < maxTicks){
    for(let k=kmin;k<=kmax;k++){
      const t = k/N, x = X(t), isInt = (k % N === 0);
      g.strokeStyle = isInt ? "#7aa2f7" : "#3d4c70";
      g.lineWidth = isInt ? 2 : 1;
      g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(x, H/2 - (isInt?14:8)); g.lineTo(x, H/2 + (isInt?14:8)); g.stroke();
      if(isInt && (kmax-kmin)/N < 14){
        g.fillStyle="#9aa8c4"; g.font="11px ui-monospace,monospace"; g.textAlign="center";
        g.fillText(String(k/N), x, H/2+30);
      }
    }
  }

  const onLattice = ((m*N) % n === 0);
  const x = X(crit);
  g.fillStyle = onLattice ? "#38d39f" : "#ff6b81";
  g.beginPath(); g.arc(x, H/2, 9, 0, Math.PI*2); g.fill();
  g.strokeStyle="#0f1420"; g.lineWidth=2; g.stroke();
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(x, H/2-9); g.lineTo(x, 26); g.strokeStyle=g.fillStyle; g.lineWidth=2; g.stroke();
  g.fillStyle = onLattice ? "#38d39f" : "#ff6b81";
  g.font="600 13px ui-monospace,monospace"; g.textAlign="center";
  g.fillText("\u2212m/n = " + fracStr(-m, n) + (onLattice ? "   \u2713 on the lattice" : "   \u2717 between ticks"), x, 18);
}

/* ---------- pole filtration ladder ---------- */
function drawFilt(){
  const {m} = state();
  const c = el("filt"), dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  const W = c.clientWidth, H = 210;
  c.width=W*dpr; c.height=H*dpr;
  const g=c.getContext("2d"); g.scale(dpr,dpr); g.clearRect(0,0,W,H);

  const show = Math.min(m, 10);
  const startK = Math.max(0, m-show);
  const rows = show+1;
  const rowH = Math.min(26, (H-40)/rows);
  const x0 = 60, wUnit = (W-160)/(show+1);

  g.font="12px ui-monospace,monospace";
  for(let i=0;i<=show;i++){
    const k = startK + i;
    const y = H - 26 - i*rowH;
    const w = wUnit*(i+1);
    const isTop = (k===m);
    g.fillStyle = isTop ? "rgba(242,177,52,.30)" : "rgba(122,162,247,.16)";
    g.strokeStyle = isTop ? "#f2b134" : "#3d4c70";
    g.lineWidth = isTop ? 2 : 1;
    g.beginPath(); g.roundRect(x0, y-rowH+5, w, rowH-4, 5); g.fill(); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle="#9aa8c4"; g.textAlign="right";
    g.fillText("Pol_"+k, x0-8, y-4);
    g.fillStyle= isTop ? "#f2b134" : "#7aa2f7"; g.textAlign="left";
    g.fillText("dim PP = "+k, x0+w+10, y-4);
  }
  g.fillStyle="#e8edf7"; g.textAlign="left"; g.font="600 12.5px ui-monospace,monospace";
  g.fillText("the product of "+m+" normalized series lives here \u2192 Pol_"+m+" \\ Pol_"+(m-1),
             x0, 18);
  if(startK>0){
    g.fillStyle="#5a6a90"; g.font="11px ui-monospace,monospace";
    g.fillText("\u22ee  (lower rungs omitted)", x0, H-8);
  }
}

/* ---------- elementary symmetric coefficients ---------- */
function esym(a){
  const m=a.length; const e=new Array(m+1).fill(0); e[0]=1;
  for(const x of a){ for(let j=m;j>=1;j--){ e[j]+= x*e[j-1]; } }
  return e;
}
function fmt(x){
  if(Number.isInteger(x)) return String(x);
  return (Math.abs(x)<1e-4||Math.abs(x)>1e6)? x.toExponential(3) : x.toFixed(4).replace(/0+$/,"").replace(/\.$/,"");
}
function drawCoeffs(){
  const raw = el("avals").value.split(",").map(s=>parseFloat(s.trim())).filter(x=>!Number.isNaN(x));
  const a = raw.slice(0,14);
  const tab = el("ctab");
  if(a.length===0){ tab.innerHTML=""; el("prodFormula").textContent="enter at least one constant"; return; }
  const m=a.length, e=esym(a);
  el("prodFormula").innerHTML =
    a.map(x=>"(q<sup>\u22121</sup> + "+fmt(x)+")").join(" \u00b7 ") +
    "  =  " +
    e.map((c,k)=>fmt(c)+"\u00b7q<sup>"+(k-m)+"</sup>").join(" + ");
  let html = "<tr><th>k</th><th>Laurent degree k \u2212 m</th><th>coefficient</th><th>e<sub>k</sub>(a)</th><th>match</th></tr>";
  for(let k=0;k<=m;k++){
    html += "<tr><td>"+k+"</td><td class='mono'>"+(k-m)+"</td><td class='mono'>"+fmt(e[k])+
            "</td><td class='mono'>"+fmt(e[k])+"</td><td class='y'>\u2713</td></tr>";
  }
  html += "<tr><td>"+(m+1)+"</td><td class='mono'>1</td><td class='mono'>0</td><td class='mono'>0</td><td class='y'>\u2713</td></tr>";
  tab.innerHTML = html;
}

/* ---------- interpolation grid ---------- */
function drawGrid(){
  const {m,n,N} = state();
  const c = el("grid"), dpr = window.devicePixelRatio||1;
  const W=c.clientWidth, H=330;
  c.width=W*dpr; c.height=H*dpr;
  const g=c.getContext("2d"); g.scale(dpr,dpr); g.clearRect(0,0,W,H);

  const NMAX=24, NROW=24;
  const padL=46, padB=30, padT=14, padR=12;
  const cw=(W-padL-padR)/NMAX, ch=(H-padT-padB)/NROW;
  for(let i=0;i<NROW;i++){
    const nn=i+1;
    for(let j=0;j<NMAX;j++){
      const NN=j+1;
      const on = ((m*NN) % nn === 0);
      g.fillStyle = on ? "rgba(56,211,159,"+(0.30+0.55*(1-i/NROW))+")" : "rgba(45,57,86,.55)";
      g.fillRect(padL+j*cw+1, H-padB-(i+1)*ch+1, cw-2, ch-2);
    }
  }
  // highlight the current cell
  if(n<=NROW && N<=NMAX){
    g.strokeStyle="#f2b134"; g.lineWidth=2.5;
    g.strokeRect(padL+(N-1)*cw+1, H-padB-n*ch+1, cw-2, ch-2);
  }
  g.fillStyle="#9aa8c4"; g.font="10.5px ui-monospace,monospace";
  g.textAlign="center";
  for(let j=1;j<=NMAX;j+=2) g.fillText(String(j), padL+(j-0.5)*cw, H-padB+13);
  g.textAlign="right";
  for(let i=1;i<=NROW;i+=2) g.fillText(String(i), padL-6, H-padB-(i-0.5)*ch+4);
  g.textAlign="center"; g.fillStyle="#7aa2f7"; g.font="11.5px ui-monospace,monospace";
  g.fillText("lattice refinement / replication depth  N", padL+(W-padL-padR)/2, H-4);
  g.save(); g.translate(12, padT+(H-padT-padB)/2); g.rotate(-Math.PI/2);
  g.fillText("exponent  n", 0, 0); g.restore();
}

/* ---------- main update ---------- */
function update(){
  const {m,n,N} = state();
  el("mLab").textContent = "m = "+m;
  el("nLab").textContent = "n = "+n;
  el("NLab").textContent = "N = "+N;
  el("mEcho").textContent = m;

  el("ordVal").innerHTML = "\u2212"+m;
  el("critVal").textContent = fracStr(-m,n);
  el("latVal").innerHTML = N===1 ? "(1/1)\u2124 = \u2124" : "(1/"+N+")\u2124";
  el("clsVal").textContent = (((-m)%n)+n)%n + " mod " + n;
  el("depthVal").textContent = n/gcd(n,m);
  el("dimVal").textContent = m;
  el("factorization").innerHTML =
    "\u220f T<sub>i</sub> = q<sup>\u2212"+m+"</sup> \u00b7 U(q),  U(0) = 1   —   "+
    "multiplying by q<sup>"+m+"</sup> restores order 0";

  const zOK  = (m % n === 0);
  const latOK= ((m*N) % n === 0);

  setVerdict("v1", zOK,
    "criterion <span class='mono'>n | m</span>: "+n+" "+(zOK?"divides":"does not divide")+" "+m+
    "  —  the critical exponent "+fracStr(-m,n)+" is "+(zOK?"an integer":"not an integer"));
  setVerdict("v2", latOK,
    "criterion <span class='mono'>n | m\u00b7N</span>: "+n+" "+(latOK?"divides":"does not divide")+" "+(m*N)+
    "  —  minimal depth for an "+n+"-th root is "+(n/gcd(n,m)));
  setVerdict("v3", latOK,
    "criterion <span class='mono'>\u2212m/n \u2208 (1/N)\u2124</span>: "+fracStr(-m,n)+" "+
    (latOK?"is":"is not")+" a multiple of 1/"+N);
  setVerdict("v4", true,
    "the value group \u211a is divisible, so \u2212m/n always exists; the root is "+
    "q<sup>"+fracStr(-m,n)+"</sup> times the binomial n-th root of U"+
    (n===m? "  \u2014 and for n = m it has order exactly \u22121" : ""));

  drawLine(); drawFilt(); drawGrid();
}

/* polyfill roundRect for older engines */
if(!CanvasRenderingContext2D.prototype.roundRect){
  CanvasRenderingContext2D.prototype.roundRect = function(x,y,w,h,r){
    this.beginPath(); this.moveTo(x+r,y); this.arcTo(x+w,y,x+w,y+h,r);
